title: Oboe Concerto in C major
hook: A 21-year-old’s concerto that was lost for over a century, hiding in plain sight as a flute concerto.

painting.title: Attributes of Music
painting.pairingNote: A horn, a violin and pipes of the kind Mozart wrote for, painted in Paris by a young artist to win her place in the Royal Academy, a few years before he set out from Salzburg to make his own name.

facts: Mozart wrote the concerto in Salzburg in 1777, when he was 21, for Giuseppe Ferlendis, an oboist from Bergamo who had just joined the Archbishop of Salzburg’s court orchestra. The orchestra is small: two oboes, two horns and strings.

That autumn Mozart left Salzburg to look for a post, and took the concerto with him. In Mannheim he gave a copy to the court oboist Friedrich Ramm. In February 1778 he wrote home that Ramm had played it for the fifth time, that it was “making a great sensation”, and that it was now Ramm’s *cheval de bataille*, his war-horse.

In 1778, short of time for a commission from a Dutch amateur flautist, Mozart seems to have turned the oboe concerto into a flute concerto, a tone higher in D major. Mozart’s own score of the oboe version was later lost.

For more than a century the work was known only as Flute Concerto No. 2. In 1920 the conductor Bernhard Paumgartner found an old set of parts for the oboe version in the archive of the Mozarteum in Salzburg, and an eight-bar sketch in Mozart’s hand, found in 1971, confirmed that the oboe came first.
bigPicture.inOneLine: a bright, open Allegro (I), a slow song like an opera [[aria|aria]] (II), a cheeky rondo whose tune Mozart later gave to a singer (III).

movements.heading: Allegro aperto
movements.summary: *Aperto* means “open” or “frank”, a marking Mozart liked at this time, and the movement is exactly that: bright, confident, in plain daylight. It is in [[sonata-form|sonata form]] with a [[double-exposition|double exposition]]: the orchestra plays the main tunes first, then the oboe enters and makes them its own. Near the end the orchestra stops for the soloist’s [[cadenza|cadenza]].

mainIdeas.name: The opening tune
mainIdeas.description: brisk and festive, full orchestra with horns, then a softer answer in the violins.

mainIdeas.name: The oboe’s entry
mainIdeas.description: one long, high note that floats above the orchestra before the oboe takes up the tune.

mainIdeas.name: The second theme
mainIdeas.description: lighter and more playful, with the oboe trading short phrases with the strings.

stops.hear: The whole orchestra, bright and brisk, then softer answers from the violins
The oboe enters on a single long, high note held over the orchestra, then runs down into the tune
The oboe sings the opening tune and decorates it with quick runs
A lighter, more playful tune; the oboe and the violins trade short phrases
A long [[trill|trill]] in the oboe, then the orchestra alone, loud and confident
stops.happening: The end of the solo exposition, marked by a [[tutti|tutti]]

stops.hear: The oboe returns; the harmony darkens for a while and wanders through minor keys
The bright opening tune again, in C major
The orchestra pauses; the oboe plays alone, leaping and racing across its whole range

stops.label: Last 20 seconds
stops.hear: The orchestra alone rounds off the movement

notice: Listen to the oboe’s first note. Instead of starting with the tune, it holds one note so long that you notice the instrument before the melody.
Compare the orchestra’s version of the opening tune with the oboe’s. The notes are the same; the oboe adds runs and turns.

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: Stankiewicz, the London Symphony Orchestra’s principal oboe, recorded the concerto live at LSO St Luke’s in London in October 2019. His cadenza in this movement is a dazzling showpiece; the one in the finale is much plainer.

movements.heading: Adagio non troppo
movements.summary: A slow song in F major, “not too slow”, that sounds like an aria from an opera with the oboe as the singer. The main melody opens with a wide leap upwards that gives it a sense of longing. After a quieter middle stretch the melody returns, and a short solo cadenza comes before the close.

mainIdeas.name: The main melody
mainIdeas.description: slow and singing, with a wide upward leap near its start.

mainIdeas.name: The second idea
mainIdeas.description: more ornamented, the oboe turning and decorating long notes.

stops.hear: Soft strings in a slow, three-beat pulse
The oboe enters quietly and sings a long melody with a wide leap upwards
The strings echo the melody, warmer and fuller
The oboe’s line becomes more decorated, with turns and long held notes
stops.happening: The second theme, in C major

stops.hear: The colour clouds over; short phrases pass between the oboe and the strings
The opening melody returns in F major
stops.happening: The return of the main theme

stops.hear: The orchestra pauses; the oboe alone spins a short, free line

stops.label: Last 30 seconds
stops.hear: Oboe and strings close quietly together

notice: Listen for the wide leap upwards in the main melody. It is the moment the song reaches out, and it comes back each time the melody does.
An oboist breathes like a singer. Notice where the long phrases pause for breath.

movements.heading: Rondo: Allegretto
movements.summary: A lively, cheeky finale. It is a [[rondo|rondo]]: a bouncy refrain keeps coming back between contrasting episodes. Five years later Mozart used almost the same tune in his opera *The Abduction from the Seraglio* (1782), for Blonde’s aria “Welche Wonne, welche Lust” (“What joy, what delight”).

mainIdeas.name: The refrain
mainIdeas.description: short, perky phrases that bounce along in two beats to a bar.

mainIdeas.name: The episodes
mainIdeas.description: quick runs and leaps for the oboe, and a central stretch that wanders into new keys.

stops.hear: The violins play a perky, bouncing tune; the whole orchestra joins in
stops.happening: The rondo refrain, played first by the orchestra

stops.hear: The oboe takes up the tune
The oboe races away with runs and leaps in a new key
The perky tune again
The music wanders through other keys, some of them minor; the instruments imitate each other
The refrain once more
The music of the first episode returns, now in C major
stops.happening: The first episode comes back in the home key

stops.hear: The orchestra stops; a short, simple solo for the oboe

stops.label: Last 30 seconds
stops.hear: The refrain one last time, then a brisk, bright close

notice: Count how many times the refrain returns. Each time, the oboe or the orchestra varies it a little.
If you know *The Abduction from the Seraglio*, listen for Blonde’s aria in the refrain.

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: The Spotify album holds the concerto twice. Tracks 1–3, the ones this guide follows, are the main version. Tracks 4–6 repeat the performance with a different cadenza in the finale, by the composer Tonia Ko.

threads.title: Oboe or flute
threads.body: The same music exists as an oboe concerto in C major and a flute concerto in D major. For more than a century only the flute version was known; today the oboe version is accepted as the original.

threads.title: The voice of an aria
threads.body: The oboe is treated like a singer throughout: long held notes, breathing phrases, a slow movement that sounds like opera. The finale’s tune later became an aria.

threads.title: A young man’s travelling music
threads.body: Mozart wrote the concerto just before leaving Salzburg to seek his fortune, and it travelled with him: to Mannheim, where it became Ramm’s war-horse, and into a flute concerto on the way to Paris.
